content: Jurisdictions classify and regulate these products as food. Supplementary foods are specifically utilized to rehabilitate individuals suffering from moderate acute malnutrition or to prevent further deterioration in their nutritional status. These interventions are particularly targeted at vulnerable groups, including children aged 6–59 months, pregnant women, and lactating mothers. Examples of such supplementary foods include corn-soy blends, wheat-soy blends, and lipid-based nutrient supplements, such as ready-to-use supplementary foods. Therapeutic foods are specially formulated products designed for the treatment of severe acute malnutrition. These include therapeutic milk formulas like F-75 and F-100, which are used during the stabilization and rehabilitation phases in inpatient settings. Additionally, ready-to-use therapeutic foods are employed during the rehabilitation phase, often in outpatient settings. The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued technical notes and guidelines on the management of moderate and severe acute malnutrition in infants and children aged 6–59 months. These guidelines are developed in collaboration with global organizations such as the World Food Programme, the United Nations System Standing Committee on Nutrition, and UNICEF. The guidelines aim to address the double burden of malnutrition, which includes both undernutrition and the rising prevalence of overweight and obesity. In 2016, global data revealed that 155 million children were stunted, 52 million were wasted, and 41 million were overweight. Undernutrition, including being underweight or stunted, is associated with increased child mortality, morbidity, and impaired development, contributing to approximately 20% of child deaths. Conversely, overweight and obesity in children have immediate physical and mental health consequences and are significant risk factors for cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and premature death in adulthood. Paradoxically, a history of low birth weight or stunting increases the risk of becoming overweight or obese and developing chronic diseases later in life. The WHO Global Strategy for Infant and Young Child Feeding emphasizes the importance of empowering health workers to provide effective feeding counseling. This is particularly critical given the magnitude of the child obesity epidemic and its link to noncommunicable diseases in adulthood. WHO guidelines aim to mitigate the risks of moderate malnutrition without inadvertently increasing the risk of obesity and related diseases in later life. The WHO Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) provides clinical algorithms for health workers at primary health-care facilities to assess and manage illnesses in infants and children, including nutritional status. Historically, IMCI has focused on preventing undernutrition, but its scope is being reviewed to address health promotion activities more comprehensively. Given the global epidemic of child obesity, IMCI guidance is being updated to contribute to efforts to end childhood obesity while addressing undernutrition. The guideline development process followed by WHO includes identifying priority questions, retrieving and assessing evidence, formulating recommendations, and planning for dissemination and implementation. The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) methodology was used to prepare evidence profiles. A steering committee and a guideline development group of experts reviewed the evidence and finalized the recommendations. The WHO emphasizes equity and human rights in health care, recognizing every child's right to grow and develop healthily. While the guideline primarily addresses clinical management within a medical model, broader contextual factors influencing health and nutrition are acknowledged but not the focus of this guideline. The guideline aims to assist Member States and partners in making evidence-informed decisions on assessing and managing children at primary health-care facilities to prevent overweight and obesity in the context of the double burden of malnutrition. It also supports efforts to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals and global nutrition targets. The recommendations prioritize three areas: (1) anthropometric assessment and classification of nutritional status, (2) management of acute or chronic malnutrition, and (3) management of overweight or obese children presenting to primary health-care facilities. The primary audience includes policymakers, program managers, health-care providers, researchers, and clinicians involved in child health and nutrition. The guideline will be reviewed and updated every 4–5 years to incorporate new evidence and ensure its relevance. WHO acknowledges the financial contributions of organizations such as the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, the Government of Luxembourg, and USAID, as well as the technical contributions of numerous individuals and institutions in developing this guideline.
